plain_english: A young man who taught rhetoric came to visit Epictetus. His hair was styled more carefully than usual and his clothes were fancy. Epictetus said to him, "Tell me — don't you think some dogs are beautiful and some horses are beautiful? And the same with all other animals?" "Yes, I do," the young man replied. "Well then, aren't some people beautiful and others ugly?" "Certainly." "Do we call them beautiful for the same reasons, or does each one have something unique that makes it beautiful? Think about it this way. We see that a dog is naturally made for one purpose, a horse for another, and a nightingale for yet another. So we can rightly say each one is beautiful when it's most excellent according to its own nature. But since each has a different nature, each one is beautiful in a different way. Isn't that right?" The young man agreed.
original_excerpt: A certain young man, a rhetorician, came to see Epictetus, with his hair dressed more carefully than was usual and his attire in an ornamental style; whereupon Epictetus said, Tell me if you do not think that some dogs are beautiful and some horses, and so of all other animals. I do think so, the youth replied. Are not then some men also beautiful and others ugly? Certainly. Do we then for the same reason call each of them in the same kind beautiful, or each beautiful for something peculiar? And you will judge of this matter thus. Since we see a dog naturally formed for one thing, and a horse for another, and for another still, as an example, a nightingale, we may generally and not improperly declare each of them to be beautiful then when it is most excellent according to its nature; but since the nature of each is different, each of them seems to me to be beautiful in a different way. Is it not so? He admitted that it was.

plain_english: What makes a dog beautiful makes a horse ugly. What makes a horse beautiful makes a dog ugly. This is true because they have different natures. Think about it this way: what makes someone good at one sport often makes them bad at another. A boxer's build might make him terrible at running. Someone perfect for one competition looks completely wrong for wrestling. So what makes a human beautiful? The same principle that makes both dogs and horses beautiful in their own way. What makes a dog beautiful? Having the excellence that belongs to dogs. What makes a horse beautiful? Having the excellence that belongs to horses. So what makes a human beautiful? Having the excellence that belongs to humans.
original_excerpt: That then which makes a dog beautiful, makes a horse ugly; and that which makes a horse beautiful, makes a dog ugly, if it is true that their natures are different. It seems to be so. For I think that what makes a Pancratiast beautiful, makes a wrestler to be not good, and a runner to be most ridiculous; and he who is beautiful for the Pentathlon, is very ugly for wrestling. It is so, said he. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it that which in its kind makes both a dog and a horse beautiful? It is, he said. What then makes a dog beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a dog. And what makes a horse beautiful? The possession of the excellence of a horse. What then makes a man beautiful? Is it not the possession of the excellence of a man?

plain_english: So if you want to be beautiful, young man, work on this: becoming an excellent human being. But what does that mean? Look at who you praise when you're being honest. Do you praise fair people or unfair people? Fair people. Do you praise people with self-control or people without it? People with self-control. Do you praise people who are disciplined or undisciplined? Disciplined people. If you make yourself that kind of person, you'll know you've made yourself beautiful. But as long as you ignore these things, you'll be ugly — no matter how hard you try to look good on the outside.
original_excerpt: And do you then, if you wish to be beautiful, young man, labor at this, the acquisition of human excellence? But what is this? Observe whom you yourself praise, when you praise many persons without partiality: do you praise the just or the unjust? The just. Whether do you praise the moderate or the immoderate? The moderate. And the temperate or the intemperate? The temperate. If then you make yourself such a person, you will know that you will make yourself beautiful; but so long as you neglect these things, you must be ugly ([Greek: aischron]), even though you contrive all you can to appear beautiful.
